label: Chapter 4: Revolt, Bombardment and Reinvention, 1568 to 1795

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the Netherlands of the sixteenth century is a powder keg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the spark comes from Spain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip the Second sends troops and a harsh general, the Duke of Alba, to put down any sign of rebellion.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Alba sets up a special court in Brussels that the locals call the Council of Blood.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It tries thousands of people for heresy and treason.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a name that tells you what you need to know.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. And it catches some very prominent people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two of the most important noblemen in the country, the Count of Egmont and the Count of Hoorn.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Both were Catholics, loyal subjects, who had only asked the king to show some moderation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that was enough.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It made no difference. On the fifth of June, 1568, Egmont and Hoorn were beheaded on a scaffold in front of the town hall, on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The execution shocked the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Egmont became a martyr, and in later centuries his story inspired a play by Goethe and an overture by Beethoven.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And politically?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It helped turn a local protest into a full-scale war.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Eighty Years' War. Long and bloody.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the north, the Dutch provinces under William of Orange eventually break away and form the Dutch Republic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the south, the fighting seesaws.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels itself joins the rebels, and for a few years in the fifteen-seventies and fifteen-eighties it's run by a militant Calvinist regime.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But in 1585, a Spanish army under the Duke of Parma retakes Brussels after a long siege.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which had consequences beyond Brussels, I think.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Big ones. Many Protestants flee north, taking their skills and their money with them, and they help build the great Dutch cities of the seventeenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The southern Netherlands, including Brussels, stays under Spanish control and stays Catholic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A border has been drawn through the Low Countries, and it's roughly the border between Belgium and the Netherlands today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wow. So one execution on a square, and eventually a country border.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's not that simple. But it's part of the story.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Did Brussels recover under the Spanish?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Slowly. From 1598 to 1621, the southern Netherlands are governed by a popular and cultured couple, the Archduke Albert and the Archduchess Isabella.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they make Brussels a glittering capital again.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Their court attracts artists, including the great Peter Paul Rubens, who paints for them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A wave of baroque churches and palaces rises across the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That sounds like a golden age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It looks like one. But Spain is in decline, and a new threat is rising in the south.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: France, under King Louis the Fourteenth, the Sun King.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh no. Not the Sun King.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Louis wants to push France's frontiers north and east, and the Spanish Netherlands lie right in his path.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For decades, French armies march back and forth across the region, and the country suffers from endless war.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then 1695.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The worst blow. August of 1695, during a conflict called the Nine Years' War.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A French army of tens of thousands, under Marshal Villeroi, marches on Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not to capture it. To punish it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Punish it? Why?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The French want to draw their enemies away from another city under siege, the fortress of Namur.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Brussels is rich and poorly defended, so it makes a tempting target.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the evening of the thirteenth of August, French cannons and mortars begin to fire red-hot shot and incendiary shells into the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bombardment goes on for about two days and nights.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The spire of the town hall is the obvious target, because it's the tallest landmark, and the shells rain down around it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the streets were narrow, and medieval.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So the fires spread. When it's over, about a third of the buildings in Brussels have been destroyed or badly damaged.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Grand Place is in ruins. All that remains of the town hall is the shell of its stone walls, still standing, the spire miraculously intact.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That must have been terrible.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the most destructive event in the city's long history.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A warning had been sent ahead, so the casualties were far fewer than they might have been.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the damage to property was staggering.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And now the part I love. Because what happens next is the best part of the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. The people of Brussels don't despair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They don't abandon the center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they don't rebuild on a brand new plan.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Instead, the guilds, which own the plots around the Grand Place, get to work.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city council and the governor require that every plan be submitted for approval.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which means the new buildings will fit together.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How long does it take?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within about four years, the square has risen again.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In stone, this time, rather than wood.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Each guildhall is a showpiece, decked with gilded statues, carvings, and symbols of its trade.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Four years. I can't get a bathroom renovated in four years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Well, they had a motivation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Stubbornness tally. This one has to be three.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Or four. Rebuilding the whole square from ash, and making it prettier?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's stubbornness with style.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So you can read the trades on the facades.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Butchers, bakers, brewers, boatmen, cabinet-makers, painters.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The house that belonged to the guild of the boatmen has a gable shaped like a ship's stern.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Another crowned its roofline with a golden phoenix, rising from the flames, as a symbol of rebirth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A phoenix. Subtle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very subtle. And all those different styles stand side by side.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Gothic, baroque, and Louis the Fourteenth styles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The mixture shouldn't work. But it does.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1998, UNESCO placed the Grand Place on its World Heritage list.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Into the eighteenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Spanish Habsburg line dies out, and after a long war of succession, the southern Netherlands pass to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1714.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the next eighty years, Brussels is the capital of the Austrian Netherlands, and the country enjoys a long period of relative peace and prosperity.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who's the beloved ruler?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Charles of Lorraine. A brother-in-law of the Empress Maria Theresa, who governs from 1744 to 1780.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A genial, sociable man who loves hunting, science, and a good table.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So, the kind of governor you'd want to have dinner with.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I think so. And under him, the city gets a makeover.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the elegant neoclassical style.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1731, the old Coudenberg Palace had been destroyed by a fire, and its ruins were cleared away and covered over.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In its place, the authorities build a handsome new district.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Place Royale, a harmonious square lined with uniform facades, and a park laid out in geometric patterns, now the Parc de Bruxelles, with straight avenues and statues.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which are among the most graceful spaces in the city today.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they date from this period.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the old order is about to crack.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Enlightenment has arrived.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the Emperor Joseph the Second, who rules from Vienna starting in 1780, tries to modernize his lands at breakneck speed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Closing monasteries, reorganizing the courts, curbing the power of the church.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And people didn't like that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many in the Austrian Netherlands, who loved their ancient privileges, are furious.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1789, the year the French Revolution begins, a rebellion breaks out in Brabant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It drives the Austrians out, and in January of 1790 a new state, the United Belgian States, is proclaimed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The first time the word Belgian appears in a country's name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the republic quickly collapses in quarrels between conservatives and democrats.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the Austrians return in December of 1790.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then France arrives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. The Austrians don't last long.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1792, French revolutionary armies march in, and after a few years of back and forth, they win a decisive victory in 1794.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1795, France formally annexes the southern Netherlands, just as it did the Duchy of Luxembourg, which became the Department of the Forests.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels becomes the capital of a French department called the Dyle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The old privileges of the Joyous Entry are swept away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The old order is gone, and Brussels, like the rest of what will become Belgium, is now part of a new France.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next time, Napoleon, Waterloo, and a night at the opera that changed the map of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which sounds like a joke. But it isn't.
